text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.
Robusta futures in London ended mixed with the most active contracts close to unchanged. Active May last traded $2 down at $1,655 per tonne, having moved from a low of $1,645 to a high of $1,683.
Arabica futures in New York posted moderate gains, but a late round of speculative selling amid news that more coffee would be finding its way to the market knocked prices off session highs.

The technical group of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) agreed on Thursday to release an additional 200,000 bags of arabica coffee to the world market in the first half of 1997. Additionally the committee decided to revoke a previous decision to reduced exports of arabica by 300,000 bags during the same period.

Most active May rose to a peak of 174.50 cents/lb before closing at 169.15 cents/lb, up 1.05 cents/lb on the day. July rose 2.30 cents/lb, to 157.20 cents/lb, while the back months closed down 0.55 to up 3.50 cents/lb. On the charts, May near-term resistance is seen at 175.00 cents/lb, with a major upside hurdle seen at 190.00 cents/lb. Support was pegged at 165.50 to 165.00, then 160.00, traders said.

ACPC - The Association of Coffee Producing Countries agreed at a technical meeting on Thursday to release an additional 200,000 bags of arabica coffee to the world market in the first half of 1997, ACPC President Rubens Barbosa of Brazil said. Barbosa said the technical committee also decided to revoke a previous decision to reduce exports of arabica coffee by 300,000 bags during the same period.

The ACPC decided in January to cut 1.3 mn bags of exports -1 mn bags of robusta and 300,000 bags of arabica. So the net effect of Thursday's decision will be a reduction of 800,000 bags of exports, Barbosa added. The ACPC full council is expected to ratify the decision by the technical committee at a meeting in May in London.

Market analysts' reactions to the decision were mixed. While some quarters consider the move to have bearish effects because it quelled fears that there is not enough coffee in the near-term, others said the additional arabica coffee may not be enough to relieve the supply crunch.

The fact that only 200,000 bags more will be available for arabica coffee seems on the low side considering the amount of front loading and of stocks and how limited exports are anticipated to be in the next two quarters, it was said. Some also believe that the newly released coffee has probably been already sold and that Thursday's decision makes it official.

UNITED STATES - After Thursday's close, the CSCE reported certified coffee stocks grew for the 11th day in a row reaching 70,529 60-kg bags as of March 19. There were an additional 13,850 pending grading, the exchange added.

SINGAPORE - Coffee imports in October 1996 amounted to 64,710 bags, down from 148,635 bags in October 1995. This brought cumulative imports in the first ten months of 1996 (January/October) up to 1.167 mn bags, almost 27 per cent down on imports recorded for the corresponding period the previous year. Total imports in 1995 reached 1.916 mn bags compared to 2.854 mn bags in 1994.

Major suppliers of green coffee in 1996 were Vietnam (140,500 vs 476,500 bags) and Laos (32,100 vs 37,200 bags). Coffee exports in October 1996 amounted to 120,748 bags, down from 173,174 bags in October 1995.
This brought cumulative exports in January/October 1996 up to 1.138 mn bags almost 30 per cent down on the tonnage exported in the corresponding period the previous year.

Total exports in 1995 amounted to 1.862 mn bags compared to 2.786 mn bags in 1994. Exports from Singapore are mainly in the form of green coffee with Malaysia (118,200 vs 116,100 bags), Australia (104,400 vs 208,100 bags) and Algeria (83,300 vs 66,600 bags) being the main markets.
